analysis.one_liner: Makes employers legally responsible for workplace harassment by anyone with power over a worker's daily duties.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had a sponsor and 17 cosponsors, was referred to four House committees but never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change who counts as a "supervisor" in workplace harassment lawsuits. In 2013 the Supreme Court limited employers' liability to harassers with the power to hire, fire, or take other formal job actions; this bill would make employers liable for harassment by anyone they let direct an employee's daily work, or where the employer's own negligence allowed the harassment. It would cover private workplaces and federal jobs, including employees of Congress itself.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who experience hostile-work-environment harassment, especially low-wage workers in retail, restaurants, health care, housekeeping, and personal care, where harassers often direct day-to-day work but lack formal hiring-and-firing authority. The bill's own findings note that women, people of color, farmworkers, older workers, and workers with disabilities are particularly affected, and that under the current narrower standard victims may have no claim against the employer for a harasser it authorized to control their daily work. It would also cover federal employees and congressional employees.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the pre-2013 standard: employers are liable for harassment by anyone they authorized to take or recommend job actions affecting the worker or to direct the worker's daily work activities, undoing the Supreme Court's Vance v. Ball State University limitation to those who can hire and fire.
Also makes employers liable when their own negligence led to the creation or continuation of a hostile work environment, adding a second, independent path to hold them responsible.

Applies the standard across the major federal anti-discrimination laws — Title VII, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Rehabilitation Act, the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act — and extends it to federal employees and to employees of Congress under the Congressional Accountability Act.

The bill's findings document why the fix targets real harm: sexual harassment made up nearly 30 percent of 2014 EEOC charges, 80 percent of surveyed female farmworkers in central California reported experiencing sexual harassment, and low-wage, female-dominated industries are where harassers most often have daily-work authority without hiring-and-firing power.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — private companies and federal agencies, including congressional employing offices — bear increased liability and litigation exposure, including the cost of defending or settling harassment claims by workers whose daily work was directed by a harasser. Businesses could also face higher insurance and compliance costs and, in some cases, more settlements.

drawbacks.text: Broader employer liability would raise litigation, settlement, and insurance costs, and smaller businesses with thinner margins would feel those costs most — an honest supporter would concede the standard shifts more risk onto employers, including those whose managers abused authority they did not fully control.
The bill applies to all claims pending on or after enactment, meaning it would change the legal rules in already-filed lawsuits midstream rather than applying only prospectively.

Supporters of the Vance decision argue that holding employers liable for people who merely direct daily work — without power to hire or fire — blurs the line between employer and co-worker misconduct, and the bill would generate more disputes over who counts as authorized to direct daily work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: the current Supreme Court standard lets a worker's employer escape liability when the person harassing her has the power to direct her every shift but no formal firing authority — a gap concentrated in exactly the low-wage, female-dominated industries the bill's findings describe. The costs are genuine but conventional: more employer litigation exposure and some uncertainty about who counts as a supervisor, softened somewhat by the bill's explicit preservation of existing defenses. The one design flaw is retroactive application to pending claims. On balance, the bill would give vulnerable workers a practical remedy at a cost mainly borne by employers' legal budgets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee from the day it was introduced — referred to four House committees and two subcommittees, none of which ever held a hearing or vote — and expired when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on July 8, 2016, with 12 original cosponsors, all House Democrats.

That same day the House referred it to four committees — Education and the Workforce, House Administration, Judiciary, and Oversight and Government Reform — meaning each would have to act on the portions in its jurisdiction before the bill could advance.

In the following weeks the bill was sent to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice (July 22) and the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Workforce Protections (September 19), a level where bills typically await hearings that decide whether they go anywhere.
The cosponsor list reached 17, all House Democrats, but no committee took up the bill, no hearing or markup is recorded, and it never reached the House floor.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing potential harassment liability are better off because the bill died: the Supreme Court's narrower Vance v. Ball State standard remains the law, so employers generally cannot be held liable for harassment by people who direct a worker's daily duties but lack hiring-and-firing authority.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.role: Sponsor, House Education and Workforce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 12 original cosponsors.

for.name: 17 of 188 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House calendar and committee chairs
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or floor vote in any of the four committees to which it was referred during the six months it was alive.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee and Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committees of primary jurisdiction, chaired by Republicans
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees but took no recorded action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote to measure, but every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat (18 of 188) and the Republican-controlled House took no action on it.

industries.industry: Private employers, especially retail, restaurant, health care, housekeeping, and personal care companies
industries.note: These industries employ many low-wage workers whose harassers often direct daily work without hiring-and-firing power — exactly the conduct the bill would newly make the employer liable for. Their interest in keeping the Vance standard is directly against workers seeking a remedy.

industries.industry: Federal agencies and congressional employing offices
industries.note: The bill would extend the liability standard to federal employees, executive branch offices, and Congress's own employing offices under the Congressional Accountability Act, exposing the government itself to more harassment claims.

industries.industry: Employment defense law firms and insurers
industries.note: More harassment claims and questions about who counts as a supervisor would mean more litigation and coverage work, though this interest is not named in the bill materials.
